rule: Stages in order: development (Mn builds), alpha, beta, then releases numbered x.y.z, with a category per major version (id "1", name "Version 1"...). Kept: development: the last build of every finished milestone and every build of the current one; releases: within a major version, the last patch of every minor version, and every patch of the newest minor version. Take the rest out of this list and run publish.py --prune.

categories.name: Development versions
categories.description: Builds made while the game was being developed, milestone by milestone (Mn); the last is nh1g (2026-11-25).

categories.name: Alpha versions
categories.description: Early versions shared with a few people: fine-tuning the game, from 2026-11-25.

categories.name: Beta versions
categories.description: Versions close to a release, for wider testing.

versions.title: Walking the open land on the minimap
versions.notes: Out on the open land it works as in a place: the minimap in the left column is how you get around. Click a region on it to travel there, W/A/S/D (marked in blue around you) walk into the next region, and the wheel zooms it. M opens the world map. "Back to the road" and "Take the road" put you out on the road instead of opening the world map, and a journey you go on with plays out on the minimap.

versions.title: The craft row's yard
versions.notes: The place to use every workshop at once is now the yard in the middle of the craft row: from there you can work at any of the row's workshops and the town's other crafting buildings (its smithy, its gem cutter's...). The workshop district's hall is only the builders' hall. The versions screen shows the newest on top: the newest category first, and its versions newest to oldest.

versions.title: Steady left column
versions.notes: The place box at the top left keeps its size whether or not the spot you stand on has a name, so the column below no longer jumps as you walk.

versions.title: Familiar calendar names
versions.notes: Options, Calendar: show familiar month and weekday names instead of Veyrath's (Monday, 14 March). The months keep their 30 days, and the names are shifted so the seasons fit: Frostwane is February, spring starts in March, and the year runs February to January.

versions.title: Save a new game's settings as defaults
versions.notes: In a new game's settings step, Save as my defaults makes what you picked there (every page) your defaults for new games, a quick way to keep a preset. It asks once more.

versions.title: Workshop districts in every town
versions.notes: The workshop district now comes before any crafter, the smithy included: every town and city has one from the start (and saves from before get theirs), so the universal bench is in every town. The W, A, S and D marks on the map are blue now, and the map's tiles have a light gap between them.

versions.title: Map ways and maps
versions.notes: The map in the left column marks W, A, S and D on the tiles around you that you can step onto. The map overview walks the safest way (around dangerous tiles) or the fastest, and a Maps tab shows the place's other maps (its buildings and their floors), with a way to their doors.

versions.title: Map overview, WASD
versions.notes: M opens a map overview of where you are: click a tile to see how long the walk is and how many dangerous tiles are on the way, then go; the places on the map (doors, ways out) are listed to go to straight away, and the world map is one press away. Out on the land M opens the world map. Walk with W, A, S and D (the arrow keys still work). The schools moved to B.

versions.title: Workshop districts
versions.notes: Towns can build a workshop district: its builders make the town's other buildings cheaper, and it opens ten crafting buildings (carpenter's shop, cookhouse, tannery, pottery, weavery, press house, distillery, mill, dye works, gem cutter's), each with its own workstation. The universal bench in the district's hall reaches every workshop built in that town.

versions.title: Category bars
versions.notes: Screens with many actions get a row of category tabs above the choices (Shift + Q / Shift + E switch): talking with people (them, hiring and household, work and trade, magic; in the conversation: getting to know them, work, the place and news, intimate) and intimate encounters (with them, your own, positions, other actions). Other screens stay as they were.

versions.title: Crafting by discipline
versions.notes: The crafting screen sorts recipes by discipline (cooking, smithing, tailoring...), what you can craft at the top. Separate splits each discipline into what you can craft and what you can't; the categories you can craft from always come first.

versions.title: More achievements count
versions.notes: Nearly every achievement can now be earned: origins, governments lived under and led, ruling, wars won and ended, realms falling, peace you made, settlements founded and grown, dungeons, crafting masterworks and draughts, performances, herds, cradle gems, children, every trait deed, schooling finished in play, the species met, the lands walked, and your records. Schooling picked at creation no longer counts, nor does a rented room as a house.

versions.title: Key labels written out
versions.notes: The choice buttons show their keys written out: 1, Shift + 1, Ctrl + 1.

versions.title: Choice keys by row
versions.notes: The choice grid's keys go by row: 1-5 the top row, Shift+1-5 the middle row, Ctrl+1-5 the bottom row.

versions.title: In at the door
versions.notes: Going into a building puts you at its entrance instead of somewhere inside, with the place's own scene as before.

versions.title: Talking, and difficulty
versions.notes: Meeting someone: the first screen has looking, gifts, hiring, business, attacking and goodbye, and "Talk with them" opens a conversation with the asking, small talk, opinions and the rest. Difficulty now does what it says: generous gives more loot and faster skills and weaker enemies, hard and brutal less loot, slower skills and tougher enemies.

versions.title: Building your home
versions.notes: What you picked to build is lit with a gold edge, and a right-click (on the list or the map) drops it. In build mode the map has an amber border and the tile under the mouse pulses. The map in the left column zooms with the mouse wheel, centred on you. Working your field or garden yourself, and the build queue, say what the work is.

versions.title: Saves, map and doors
versions.notes: Saves can be deleted: a Delete mode on the save screen, asking once more. Double-click a region on the world map to travel there. Walking onto a door or a way out no longer takes you through at once: the choice to go in or leave comes first in the list (or click the tile again).

versions.title: Fixes from hand testing
versions.notes: Lust is listed below stamina. Creation's Back asks before leaving for the main menu. People with common jobs are "a mercenary", not "the mercenary here". Action tooltips set the name apart and give the time in words. Options: metric and imperial listed apart, a live sample for the scene text size, the interface size follows the slider live without un-maximizing the window, and leaving fullscreen goes back to a maximized window.

versions.title: Records page fix
versions.notes: The records page no longer squeezes "none yet" and the numbers into one letter a line.

versions.title: Achievements and unlocks
versions.notes: Achievements arrive: a window on the main menu and in the game menu with a counter, sections, secret achievements that reveal themselves as you find more, and your records across all lives. A new profile now starts with creation and the world options limited (the smallest world, human, the amnesiac...) and achievements open the rest; an existing profile stays fully unlocked (a switch in the window, earning nothing). The first deeds count already: guild ranks (with a new Platinum rank), trades, years lived, a house, schooling, the cold and hot lands, your first spell and fight, dungeons cleared.

versions.title: Where colours show
versions.notes: The character overview says where each colour shows in a few words (the whole body, most of the body, head and tail, hair) instead of listing every part, inner ones too.

versions.title: Option texts
versions.notes: World options explain the option you chose, with its numbers, instead of listing every option (world size, age, population, climate, dungeons, kind of world and more). Content options now go Content, Species, World, then the adult pages; the Content page goes Ways of life, Bodies (skin colours first), Hair. Each page says what it is about. Ticked boxes no longer vanish under the mouse. Gem incubation no longer mentions an old milestone and is told apart from the cradle keeper.

versions.title: Scrolling fixes
versions.notes: Lists that go on further down show it: a shadow at the bottom ending in a black line. A little more room between the scrollbar and the text and buttons. A slider under the mouse now takes the mouse wheel before the list around it, both ways, so scrolling back undoes an accidental change instead of moving the page.

versions.title: New game in two steps
versions.notes: Character creation is one step now, its sections as buttons to switch between; Next walks them, then shows the new game's content options to fine-tune before Create the world. Content options are reordered: a new Content page first (ways of life, bodies, hair, skin colours), then Species, then World. With adult content off, adult options are hidden, but not hair and other non-adult ones. Extended creation is gone: its options come from your profile (all open for now).

versions.title: Profile for achievements
versions.notes: The groundwork for achievements: your player profile is now kept beside your settings, outside the saves, ready to record achievements across all your worlds and lives and what they unlock. For now everything stays open (a fully unlocked profile) while the unlocks are worked out.

versions.title: Faster years in a growing world
versions.notes: A speed-up: with hamlets growing into villages and towns, years had grown slow, because every town's merchant history was worked out again from the world's start whenever a settlement grew or any place came or went. Now only the merchants near a change rethink their routes, and only from this year on. In a 10k world the slowest year went from 28 seconds to 7, and the nearby towns' yearly business is spread over the month instead of one day.

versions.title: Conquest, world age, schools, daily life
versions.notes: Four parts in one. Realms that conquer: ambitious rulers go for conquest, a realm that grows too big and too fast has its neighbours rise against it together, and a realm with nowhere left to expand builds up its towns, then looks for land by treaty or war; realms born later now meet the realms around them. World age: a new option beside the size, from fresh (only free folk, no ruins) to ancient (more anima, more and deeper dungeons, more ruins, five years of history before you arrive). Schools and universities: pick your schooling at creation, enrol later at a town's school, high school or university, and work that asks for it opens; three years in a realm's army count too. Daily life: small talk, shops that keep hours, a gentle tiredness that sleep clears, two meals a day and a night's sleep keep you Fed and rested, the town's weather and season and nights, things that happen in your work shifts, evenings with your family, walking the streets at night.

versions.title: Hamlets grow into villages
versions.notes: Families in steadings and hamlets now build their own homes, a few a year while they are short of room, instead of the settlement paying for every house. Before, a hamlet spent all it earned on houses it never caught up with, so it never built the shrine a village needs; crowded, its people left to found yet more steadings. Now hamlets grow into villages.

versions.title: Every realm has an army
versions.notes: Small realms had no army at all: their troops rounded down to nothing, so most wars were declared with no one to fight them and nobody ever needed mercenaries. Now even the smallest realm plans a troop of levies, filled at war as far as its people allow, and a realm plans its armies again as it grows. Wars are fought and end sooner, and realms short of soldiers hire mercenary troops.

versions.title: Faster new dungeons
versions.notes: A speed-up: when a dungeon opens, the free places for it found by the last search are used for a month instead of searching the whole map again each time. In worlds where adventurers clear dungeons often this took most of a second a year; now about a tenth of that.

versions.title: Deposits on the Minerals map
versions.notes: Settlements founded after the world was made now know the deposits around them, as the first towns always did, so the Minerals map shows them (in a world begun with only free folk it showed nothing). Zoomed out on a large world the map shows deposits too, and the observer's runs show every deposit, known or not.

versions.title: Dungeons in a full world
versions.notes: A speed-up: once a world has no free place left for a new dungeon, it no longer searches the whole map for one on every day a dungeon could open, only once a month. In a crowded world this saved most of a second a year.

versions.title: Mercenary troops
versions.notes: A realm at war whose armies are weaker than its enemies' now hires mercenaries troop by troop into its own armies, from the free companies near its land: a fee up front and pay by the month to the company, which keeps the rest of its soldiers and carries on as a free company. When the war ends, the hired troops go back to their company.

versions.title: Fair battles
versions.notes: Two equal armies now win about half the time each. Before, when neither side broke and the battle went on to dusk, the enemy's commander always got to rally a wavering line and yours often didn't, so even fights, above all with levies, were nearly always lost. Now both rally before dusk, an enemy's commander by their leadership as yours is. Levies stay weaker than drilled troops: an equal number of standing soldiers beats them.

versions.title: Regard on borders
versions.notes: When a refugee wave reaches another realm, the realm they fled remembers what it found there: an open border makes it think better of that neighbour, a closed one worse, more for a bigger wave (up to 10 regard).

versions.title: Chimes
versions.notes: Money has a name now: chimes. Every price, wage, fee and treasury is ten times what it was, so there are no fractions left (a loaf is 20 chimes, not half a coin), and your saves are converted when you load them, purse and all. Fees that came up in more than one place are kept in one price table, so a meal or a bed at an inn costs the same everywhere.

versions.title: Every trade in the economy
versions.notes: The town's trades now make their own goods for the market: tailors the clothes, cobblers the boots and shoes, carpenters the furniture, coopers the barrels, chandlers the candles and soap, butchers the meat, healers the salves and bandages, masons the bricks and mortar, and scribes paper talismans and scrolls, each with a spell of its own. Prices follow who lives where: clothes are cheap in a town of tailors. Ask a tradesperson about their work to hear how many hands they keep and whether they have an apprentice, whom you can meet; and if your employer dies, their apprentice may carry on and keep you on.

versions.title: Scrolls teach a spell
versions.notes: A scroll now teaches one particular spell or technique, the one written in it: read it and you know it, as long as its school is already open to you and you don't know the spell yet; otherwise nothing happens and you keep the scroll. Scrolls no longer give school points: those come from using a school's spells and abilities. Scribes copy scrolls of all sorts of spells, and any old school scroll you had now teaches the next spell of its school you don't know. The scroll of tongues is now a talisman.

versions.title: Scrolls and talismans, set right
versions.notes: Scrolls are once again only what unlocks a school's spells and abilities, and now every school has one. The one-use written spells are paper talismans alone: scribes copy scrolls and brush talismans, you make your own talismans from paper and cinnabar in the spellbook, and any one-use scroll you had is a talisman now. Talismans and the odd scroll also turn up in dungeon hoards, and on people you beat in a fight.

versions.title: Writing your own scrolls
versions.notes: Write your own scrolls and paper talismans from the spellbook: any spell or technique you know, poured into the page at its usual cost. A scroll needs vellum, parchment or paper and ink; a talisman paper and cinnabar. Your skill and the material decide how good it comes out, and the scribes' stall now sells the paper, ink and cinnabar.

versions.title: Scrolls and paper talismans
versions.notes: Scribes now write scrolls and paper talismans of every school, magical and martial: each holds one spell or technique that anyone can use once, with no mana and no learning. Read a scroll aloud and its words burn off the page; burn a talisman's yellow paper, paste it on, or drink its ash in water. Talismans are quicker in a fight, scrolls stronger. Find them at the scribes' stall on any market (a new batch every few days), and talismans of warding and healing at the temple.

versions.title: Broken bones
versions.notes: Playing with lasting injuries, a lost fight can now break an arm, crack your ribs or twist a knee as well as leave a deep wound, and they take weeks to heal on their own. A healer at the healer's house or the temple can set them so they mend in a couple of days.

versions.title: Sickness at home
versions.notes: Your family and household can fall ill too: they keep to bed for a few days and do no work, and the day's report tells you who is ill and who is well again. At the healer's house or the temple you can send a healer to them for a few coins each.

versions.title: A wedding feast
versions.notes: Betrothed? You can now hold the wedding with a feast for the whole town: long tables, a roast, a fiddler, and half the town dancing. It costs more in a bigger place, and the town thinks the better of you for it.

versions.title: Another guild's turf
versions.notes: Thieves' guilds now guard their crowds: pick pockets where a guild works that isn't yours, and its enforcers may find you, take what you lifted and leave you a bruise. Join the guild there, or be very quiet.

versions.title: The college of magic, room to grow
versions.notes: Cities now have a college of magic, where masters of fire, water, earth, air and the arcane lecture each day for a few coins. And settlements are no longer limited by the lots on their maps: buildings that don't fit stand in a new quarter, so the healer's house, the school and the rest all show.

versions.title: Working your passage
versions.notes: Short of the fare? At a port, sign on as a deckhand from the work board: your next voyage costs nothing, and when you make port you're paid a hand's wage for every day at sea.

versions.title: Falling ill
versions.notes: You can now fall ill now and then: a fever, a bad cough or the flux, more often in crowded towns and cities, when you're worn out, or after tending the sick, and less if you're hardy. They pass in a few days, or a healer at the healer's house or the temple can break them for a few coins; a tincture eases a cough, and theriac cures them all.

versions.title: Stolen goods and the fence
versions.notes: What you steal is now marked as stolen, and honest shops and merchants won't buy it. In the back alleys of towns where a thieves' guild works there's a fence who takes anything, for a thief's price; and a job for the guild sometimes brings you a candlestick, a ring or a gem to sell there.

versions.title: Patrons, acolytes and the watch
versions.notes: Nobles now keep a musician: a good enough bard can win a patron and rise to court bard. Priests take acolytes, who can rise to priest of the temple; watch captains hire watchmen; and stewards take on clerks. Ask them, or answer their openings on the work board.

versions.title: The healer's house and the school
versions.notes: The healer's house now opens its door: have your wounds seen to, buy bandages, salves and tinctures, or go round the sick with the healer. And in towns with a school you can spend a few hours a day in its reading room for a couple of coins, and come out the wiser.

versions.title: A quieter town square
versions.notes: The town square has far fewer buttons: your job's choices (going to work, your masterwork, your trade's guild, leaving) are on one "Your work" page; crying your wares and picking pockets are on the market; and towns and cities have back alleys on their maps, where the thieves' guild is found.

versions.title: Magic for hire, scholars
versions.notes: The work board now has work for those with magic: warding houses, calling rain on fields, healing by magic, lighting streets, enchanting tools. A magister takes on a mage's assistant, to become a journeyman and a master mage; towns and cities have scholars who take on clerks; and with adult content, pleasure houses take on hands. Answering a board's opening no longer needs the tradesperson to know you first.

versions.title: The sick and the square
versions.notes: At the temple you can now do a round of the town's sick with a bandage, a salve or laudanum, paid by their families; and on the market you can play in the square by day for the passers-by.

versions.title: The thieves' guild
versions.notes: Pick pockets in the crowds of towns and cities, at the risk of a hand on your wrist and the watch's fines. Where the outlaws keep a thieves' guild, seek it out and join: its lookouts watch your back, it takes its cut, it has jobs for you by night, and you can rise from cutpurse to master thief.

versions.title: Your own field
versions.notes: Work your own field or garden yourself: four hours of your hands bring in what a hired farmer or gardener would, more with your skill, straight into your stores.

versions.title: Festivals
versions.notes: Four festivals a year: the Spring Fair, Midsummer, the Harvest Home and the Longest Night. Join in to rest and be seen among the townsfolk, try the wrestling, archery, baking or singing contest for a prize, and sell twice as much in your shop or in the streets that day.

versions.title: Letters and parcels
versions.notes: The work board now posts letters and parcels to carry to settlements a few regions away, paid by the distance when you arrive there in time.

versions.title: Hunting and fishing
versions.notes: Out in the open land you can now go hunting, and fish wherever there is water. What you catch depends on what lives there and how much game the land still holds, and on your hunting skill; hunt a place out and it takes a while for the game to come back.

versions.title: Openings on the work board
versions.notes: Each week the work board posts openings: a baker, a miller, a tailor or another tradesperson of the town who wants a hand, or a master who takes an apprentice. Answer one and you are taken on, even by the trades you could not find to talk to before. And you can now leave your work, present your masterwork or join your trade's guild from the town itself.

versions.title: A soldier's troop
versions.notes: Enlisting now puts you in one of the army's troops: your own people's if it has one (a centaur rides with the centaur cavalry), otherwise by what you are best at, archers for a bowman, mages for a mage, the foot for a fighter. And the ranks climb further, from soldier through corporal, sergeant and lieutenant to captain.

versions.title: Orders
versions.notes: Ask townsfolk if they need anything made: a guard wants a blade, a noble a fine gown, an innkeeper chairs, a farmer tools. Make it well enough and bring it within the days they give, and they pay well above its worth and think better of you; let it lapse and they remember that too.

versions.title: Crying your wares
versions.notes: Take what you have baked or sewn out into the streets and cry your wares: passers-by stop you to buy, more in a big town and on market day. And bakers can now make meat pies, apple tarts, honey cakes and fruit buns, which only shops and street sellers sell.

versions.title: Craft guilds
versions.notes: Towns and cities now have a guild for each craft. Once you are a journeyman or master of a trade, you can join its guild in a town for a fee and monthly dues: guild members' shops get more of the town's custom, outsiders' less.

versions.title: More trades, market days, body age
versions.notes: Towns now have tailors, cobblers, carpenters, coopers, chandlers, butchers, healers, midwives, scribes, masons, barbers, teachers, carters and launderers among their people; each takes on hands, and the crafts among them take apprentices. Every settlement holds a market on a weekday of its own, with busier shops and more odd jobs. And your body's age is now kept apart from the years you have lived: magic can make you younger or older in body, and a change of species keeps the share of life you have left.

versions.title: A shop of your own, a family's wages
versions.notes: Build a shopfront in your house in town, mark what you make for sale, and mind the shop yourself or have someone keep it: townsfolk come in and buy at the town's prices. Bake bread in your kitchen and sell it, and live off it. Those who live with you can also work in town for wages into your home's coffer, and when you go on as your heir, your old job and trade titles end with you.

versions.title: A house in town
versions.notes: Buy or rent a house inside a village, town or city from its reeve or elder, instead of a plot outside it. Go home from the streets into your hall, build and furnish rooms, keep a household there. Rent is paid each week from the house's coffer or your purse; fall too far behind and you will be put out, with your things.

versions.title: Apprenticeship
versions.notes: Pay a master smith, baker, weaver, potter or another craftsman a premium to take you as their apprentice: work for pocket money while you learn the craft much faster, and after twelve weeks become a journeyman. A skilled journeyman can present a masterwork and become a master. Your title goes with you to any workshop of the trade.

versions.title: The work board
versions.notes: Every village, town and city now has a work board with a few odd jobs each day: a morning at the bakery, unloading a wagon, mucking out the stables, minding a stall, chopping firewood and more. A few hours' work, paid at once, for when you are starting out with nothing.

versions.title: Being employed
versions.notes: Ask a smith, a baker, an innkeeper, a farmer or one of many other townsfolk for work, and they may take you on as a hand. Work your shifts in their hours, get paid at the end of each week, rise in rank with a raise when you are well thought of, and be let go if you stop turning up. Your job, your wage and payday show in the town.

versions.title: Wars that end
versions.notes: Wars between clans of the free folk no longer drag on for ten years with every border village fighting its neighbours each month: the longer and bloodier a war, the likelier its sides make peace, and a clan war goes on as a proper war between realms once both clans have become realms.

versions.title: Far-off bands raid in step
versions.notes: Hungry bands of the free folk far from you now raid their neighbours as often as those close by. With this, the world far away and the world near you now grow alike: over fifty years and three different worlds, their people, settlements, realms, fights, births and deaths all came out within a few percent of each other.

versions.title: Far-off clans in step
versions.notes: Clans of the free folk far from you now draw in bands and merge with their neighbours as often as those close by, instead of a third as often, so the world far away no longer splinters into twice as many little realms as it should. Those who wintered in a distant village no longer miss their spring departure, and distant feuds can flare more than once in a season.

versions.title: Mercenaries in proportion; smoother travels
versions.notes: Mercenary companies no longer conjure followers out of nothing: their families, smiths and cooks now come from the towns near their camp, at most about one for each soldier, and settle in the nearest town when there are too many or the company breaks up. Travelling into new lands no longer brings a long pause while every merchant around is worked out at once; their caravans appear over the next hours instead. On a well-travelled endless world a year now passes in a sixth of the time it took before the lands far away began to wait, with much shorter pauses, and wild game and the free folk's search for a town to winter in are cheaper too.

versions.title: Endless worlds: far lands wait for you
versions.notes: On an endless world, the lands you have left far behind now wait for you: their realms, free folk, dungeons and beasts stand still until you come near again, and then catch up on what they would have done in the meantime, so a realm's treasury has grown by its months of taxes. After travelling six continents east, a year of the world now passes in about a third of the time it took before, with much shorter pauses. New endless worlds also place their towns and villages as people would. Realms' diplomacy is faster on large worlds too.

versions.title: Far-off clans and feuds; news from afar
versions.notes: Far from you, the free folk's clans and feuds now move at a slower pace, the farther the slower, while still growing into tribes and realms and fighting their wars. What happens far away now reaches you as a summary each season, by direction ('Word from the far north: three villages founded, two bands split...'), while the big turns, such as a new realm, a war or a massacre, are told at once. Villages founded far away join the nearest clan of their own tongue. This also fixes a crash when a distant band whose named members had all died tried to join a settlement.

versions.title: Rings of detail: the world far away as numbers
versions.notes: Far from you, the world no longer follows every wanderer one by one. Within about a week's travel everything lives as before. Further out, bands keep only their leaders and the people you have met as persons, the rest as counts of each people by age and sex, so their mix of peoples is kept; they move, fight, split, settle and join towns more slowly. Beyond that, the roaming free folk become numbers per district, born, dying, drifting toward better land and founding villages, and they form bands again as you come near. On a large world this makes the free folk's years about twice as fast. The simulation tests can now run either in full detail everywhere or as a player would see it.

versions.title: Refugees never turn to crime
versions.notes: Refugees nobody takes in no longer drift into banditry: a small group crowds into the nearest town anyway, and a larger one founds a village of its own on free land or takes to the road as a band. Only true outlaws, such as broken soldiers or those turned away at a border, form gangs. This ends a loop in which people left the gangs as refugees only to turn bandit again.

versions.title: Realms take in refugees; gangs dwindle and are hunted
versions.notes: Refugees that no nearby town can take in are now resettled by the realm whose land they are in, in any of its towns with homes to spare, or given land for a village of their own. Bandit gangs no longer hold their people forever: some leave them every year for ordinary lives, and the realms around find their hideouts and break them, more surely where their armies are strong; about half of a broken gang's people come back as refugees. This also fixes a rare crash when refugees arrived just as a crowded village sent out settlers.

versions.title: Fewer outlaws, more villages
versions.notes: Whole peoples were quietly vanishing into bandit gangs: refugees from crowded villages that no town could take in turned to crime by the thousands. Now a crowded village of the free folk sends its extra people out to found a daughter village when there is land, refugees nobody takes in found a village of their own or take to the road as a band again, and only those near a realm's towns turn to crime. A bandit gang remembers how many people it took in, and when it is broken about half of them come back as refugees. Long games also stay faster: the danger of a place no longer looks through every beast ever slain and every dungeon ever cleared. The simulation tests bring every town up to date over each month, so their births and populations are counted truly.

versions.title: Settled as people would; installed sizes and the installer
versions.notes: Settlements are no longer placed the way a planner would. Wandering folk pick where to go by chance among the places they know, favouring better land but not always the best; they are drawn toward their kin and the roads, and each leader has a taste of their own, for high ground, the water's edge, the woods, open land or crossroads. New worlds also spread their towns and villages less evenly, with villages gathering around the towns. Saved worlds stay as they were. The version list now shows how much room each version takes once installed, beside its download size, and the game is ready for a standalone installer that installs any version and then removes itself.

versions.title: Ruins and the abandoned
versions.notes: When a settlement is abandoned, its last people now leave as refugees and are taken in by the towns nearby, rather than wandering off as a band. What they leave behind is a ruin: its buildings crumble year by year while it lies empty, and in time settlers can move in and make it a home again, whether a band looking for land, a crowded town's daughter village, refugees with nowhere else to go, or a realm raising an outpost on the road. The simulation tests now also count refugees, mercenaries and outlaws, so everyone is accounted for.

versions.title: Everyone counted in the simulation tests; threats kept apart from the slain
versions.notes: The simulation tests now count everyone: alongside the free folk, the people of the realms' towns (where bands that accept a realm's rule go to live) and the soldiers in the forts, with a total, so it shows that no one goes missing. And the game no longer looks through every beast and bandit ever slain whenever it checks the threats about, which made long games slower year by year.

versions.title: Cost trims: rulers' projects; a map for mercenary camps
versions.notes: Rulers thinking up projects for their capitals now glance at what the capital last made, rather than working out its whole year's trade again, which halves the time the realms take each month; a medium world's year now runs in under five seconds. Mercenary camps also have a map of their own now, with tents, horse lines and the captain's pavilion, so you can walk into one.

versions.title: Cost trims: a glance at a town
versions.notes: A normal world's years run two to three times faster. Free folk deciding whether a town would take them in, and realms counting what their smiths make for their soldiers, now glance at what the town's people and land make, without first working out the trade of every merchant who might visit it. And a realm changing its laws on magic now only makes its own towns work out their trades again, not every town in the world. On a medium world the second year of a game now takes about 6 seconds, where it took 15.

versions.title: Cost trims: founding and the forts' recruits
versions.notes: Two slow spots in a normal world's days are gone. When a settlement, mine or quarry is founded or abandoned, only the settlements near it work out their trades again, not every one in the world. And when a realm sends its towns' recruits to its forts each month, the towns no longer have to be brought fully up to date first. The forts' recruiting now takes a fiftieth of the time it did, and the slowest day of a year is less than half as long.

versions.title: Births and deaths in every settlement
versions.notes: Settlements now have births and deaths of their own, rather than one net growth figure: about four in a hundred people are born each year (more in a contented town, and more where a priest sees to the births) and about one and a half in a hundred die (fewer where a priest cares for the sick, more where people are crowded in). The simulation tests record both for every settlement and chart them beside those who left and arrived.

versions.title: Free folk redo: bands, refugees, outlaws and mercenaries
versions.notes: Wandering bands now come to terms with the realms whose land they roam. A band that stays in a realm's land may accept its rule, more readily if its leader is easy-going, if the realm's towns are of its own people and if the realm treats its kind well; a proud band refuses. A band that has accepted slowly settles into the realm's nearest towns, a tenth of it each month, its notable people becoming townsfolk there, until it is no more. A band that refuses is an outsider eating the realm's food: the realm's soldiers drive it off, and a band beaten again and again breaks up and is taken in. People who leave a crowded town no longer become wandering bands: they gather as refugees around it and settle month by month in the towns nearby that have room, wandering further as time goes on. A large crowd of refugees makes the roads around it less safe and the towns beside it uneasy, and if it grows too big it marches on the capital as a refugee wave, or across the border to a neighbouring realm, which may take them in or close its border. Those turned away scatter, some of them into outlaws. Refugees who linger too long, and outlaws who gather (turned away, or deserters from a broken army), turn to crime: in a town, a thieves' guild that grows on the refugees, skims the town's building fund, spreads to the next town and is cracked down on by the realm's soldiers; in the wild, a bandit gang with a hidden hideout that robs the villages around until you stumble on it or the realm's patrols find it. Some take up the sword instead: fighting bands with ambitious leaders, and soldiers left without an army, form mercenary companies with camps of their own on the map. A company earns its keep guarding the land around and hunting beasts and bandits for their bounties, and in wartime realms hire it for a fee to fight on their front; its followers may settle a hamlet by the camp in time, and a company left idle and unpaid too long turns outlaw.

versions.title: Army redo, part 5: soldiering, the front lines and garrisons
versions.notes: You can enlist again: join one of a realm's armies at its home town (the realm's screen). In peacetime you serve and are paid while free to travel; when war comes you march with your army to its front and fight in its battles, which are fought round by round with you in the line, and their outcome decides the battle on that front. Your own army at your liege's front fights the same way. Near a war's front the roads change: enemy patrols stop travellers, and bands of deserters camp off the road. Visiting a fort now shows its garrison as real troops (spearmen, archers, riders) under a named captain.

versions.title: Army redo, part 6: no more marching realm armies
versions.notes: Realms no longer send armies marching across the map day by day: everything is done by their planned armies. Risings in their towns are put down by the armies stationed near, week by week, much as threats are hunted. A rebel lord is met on a front at the rebels' seat, and one battle there decides whether the rebellion is crushed or holds on. When your liege goes to war, your army is called to its front: answer, march there, and it fights alongside your liege's armies until the peace. Armies from older saves are sent home. Enlisting as a soldier in a realm's army has nothing to join for now; it returns with a later part.

versions.title: Army redo, part 4: war on the fronts
versions.notes: Wars are now fought between the realms' planned armies on their fronts. When war comes, each realm calls up its levies from its towns (each town gives up to two in five of its people, as far as it likes the realm) and sends its armies to the front, where they arrive after their march. Each month on a front brings skirmishes or a battle; the stronger side usually wins, and a beaten army's troops may break, some going home, some turning outlaw (enough of them become a warband). The side ahead besieges the enemy's nearest town, which holds out by its stores and its defences. A war stance decreed before the war makes a realm's armies hit harder in a war it starts, or hold better in one started against it. At peace the levies go home. When you rule, you choose each army's front.

versions.title: Army redo, parts 2 and 3: armies fill, and guard the land
versions.notes: Planned armies now fill. Towns build conscription offices, and each month their officer draws recruits, as many as the realm's conscription allows, into the standing troops of the armies based nearby. Their gear comes from the realm's own smiths and workshops, or from merchants at a higher price; a recruit without gear trains and fights at half strength until it arrives. Soldiers are paid each month; a realm deep in debt takes on no more and some desert. Realms no longer keep standing armies marching on the map. Levies still wait for a war. A realm's armies now guard its land from their home towns: their presence is strongest at home and fades with distance (a new Presence map view shows it), making the roads safer. Each week a threat in a realm's land may be hunted by one of its armies, more likely where they are strong; a threat that beats them is reckoned more dangerous, the realm comes back with more armies, and the bounty on it grows.

versions.title: Army redo, part 1: planned armies
versions.notes: Realms now plan their armies: each has a commander with leadership, tactics, logistics and a trait, a home town, and troops of the kinds the realm can actually raise, whether levies called up for war or standing troops. The plans don't fill yet; that comes next. New troops: levy spearmen and levy archers (farmers with their own weapons) and knights, raised only where a realm has a city. When you rule a realm, its screen lets you plan armies yourself: pick a home and a commander, add troops within what the commander can lead, and confirm.

versions.title: Homes keep up
versions.notes: Towns now build as many homes as their people need. Before, a town built at most a few buildings a year whatever it was, so houses fell behind the births while the building funds piled up, and more people left each year than were born. Now new houses go up as the town grows, and people stay unless the farms can't keep them.

versions.title: Standing armies fill their ranks
versions.notes: A realm's forts now fill their ranks from the realm's own towns, a little each month, and stop drawing once they are full. How many may be called up a month follows the realm's conscription: a trickle of volunteers, more under the levy, the most under a full levy. Crowded towns send their extra hands first. Soldiers no longer appear from nowhere, and towns no longer lose people every year to garrisons that are already full; in peacetime, soldiers beyond the ranks are sent home to the realm's towns.

versions.title: A much faster normal world
versions.notes: A normal world runs about ten times faster. Every time a cave or a rift opened or closed somewhere in the world, which happens almost daily, the game threw away what every settlement makes and worked it all out again, more than a second each time. Now only new or lost settlements, mines and quarries do that. Armies, travellers, realms and the settlements' years all felt it: armies most, since a town missing its levies needed that work every day.

versions.title: Simulation tests: normal worlds
versions.notes: The simulation tests can now watch a normal game, not only an empty world of free folk: a new game started as a player would start it, on a small, medium or large map, with a dummy character beginning where a new player begins. Pick the population (sparse, normal or crowded) in place of the number of free folk. Besides the free folk's figures, a normal world's run records the whole world year by year: its settlements and their people (born, left, arrived, by size, crowded, founded, ruined), realms and war (loyalty, wars, armies, sieges, towns changing hands), the economy (food kept, grain prices, travellers, building funds) and what a player would find around the dummy's home town, with three more charts.

versions.title: Settlements keep growing
versions.notes: Settlements no longer hold themselves back by having fewer children when food runs short: people have children every year whatever the harvest, and the town's head puts the extra hands on the fields first. Families crowd into the homes there are, and a crowded town grows unhappy; past what its farms or homes can keep, people leave. Those who leave no longer vanish: some take to the roads as bands, and the rest move to towns nearby with food and homes to spare, their own realm's first. Crowded villages now feed the towns around them and the wild.

versions.title: No hunger, part 5: animals and the last of it
versions.notes: Your animals no longer wander off when there is nothing to feed them: an unfed beast gives no milk, eggs or wool (a little, with good husbandry) until it is fed again, but it stays with you. Bound spirits and wild creatures still leave if neglected. The siege plan Starve them out is now Wear them down, and a besieged town shows how many days of supplies it has left. The last talk of hunger is gone from companions, army leaders and notices. Saves from before the hunger changes load and carry on.

versions.title: No hunger, part 4: the free folk
versions.notes: The free folk no longer starve. A band still gathers, hunts and keeps stores, but when its land can't keep it and the stores run out it has lean days instead of hungry ones: no one dies or sickens of want, the band grows unhappy, has fewer children the further it is over what the land can carry, and moves on, splits, raids its neighbours or makes for a settlement. In autumn, bands on land where the winter bites hard, or with too little laid by, look for a settlement to winter in. The free folk screen now says whether the land provides, is stretched, or the band is in lean times.

versions.title: No hunger, part 3: armies and sieges
versions.notes: Armies no longer go hungry. Their supplies are now supplies of war (arrows, repairs, medicine and fodder), and they matter only when your realm is at war and the army is away from home; at peace or on your own land, its upkeep keeps it supplied. Out of supply, an army fights worse, loses heart and some soldiers slip away, but no one starves. Foraging is now requisitioning: it still strips the land and angers the towns nearby. Granaries are war stores: a town's granaries carry its supply line further. In a siege the stores are supplies, and a priest keeping the peace steadies the defenders. The monthly levy work is now spread over the month, so there is no more pause on one day.

versions.title: No hunger, part 2: you, your party and household
versions.notes: You and your companions never need to eat any more: no daily meals on the road, no hunger, and journeys no longer stop when the food runs out. A supper at camp is now a pleasure that leaves everyone well fed and in better spirits, from a cook, a forager's finds or a little food from your packs. Cooked food now gives buffs by its kind: meat dishes make you hearty, bread and cheese keep you going, smoked fish sharpens the mind, sweets put you in a good humour, and drink makes you merry; raw food just restores a little stamina, and the inn's hot meal is hearty. Your household's keep is now paid in coins, and a well-stocked kitchen keeps them happy.

versions.title: No hunger, part 1: settlements by capacity
versions.notes: Settlements no longer starve. Each keeps as many people as its farms, herds and fishing can comfortably support, more as it grows into a town or city; its head puts more people to the fields when it nears the limit, and when it is past it, people leave for other places instead of dying. Granaries now hold a reserve that tides a town over bad years and lets it take in winter guests, sell grain when it has plenty, and steady its grain prices. Priests can now also care for the sick, for mothers and newborns, comfort a town through hard years, and keep the peace. Towns are described as crowded or overcrowded instead of hungry or starving.

versions.title: Herders in the open
versions.notes: Out in the open you may now come across herders with their herds: shepherds on the plains and steppe, goatherds in the hills, cattle drovers on the savanna and wet grasslands, reindeer herders in the north and camel herders in the deserts. They are most likely on good pasture near settlements that keep herds, and rare far from any. You can share their fire and hear news of the land, or buy a sheep or a goat for your own herd. Large free folk worlds also run a little faster again.

versions.title: Free folk: wild food as the land's own
versions.notes: Game and wild plants are now part of the land itself: each region holds as much game as its grazing feeds in the season, which regrows when hunted and drifts toward the warm land in winter, and its gathering recovers after it is picked. Wandering bands and settlements' hunters and gatherers draw on the same land and compete for it, so new settlements now spread further apart instead of crowding onto land that is already worked. Bands live their days a few at a time, which makes large worlds faster again, and settlements take in bands even when they have homes for only part of them.

versions.title: Free folk: no more monthly hitch
versions.notes: The free folk's monthly work no longer all happens on the first day of the month: each band, settlement and clan now takes its turn on its own day, so the work is spread evenly and the game no longer stalls for a second or more once a month in large worlds. Simulation tests in the observer also run faster, since the window no longer waits for the screen at the fastest speed, and each run now records its longest day and what took the time.

versions.title: Free folk: faster once they settle
versions.notes: Large free folk worlds no longer slow down as their people settle. Clans, settlements and bands looking for a place to live used to redo far more work each month the more settlements there were; with over a thousand settlements a simulated year took nearly two minutes. That work is now done once a month and kept up to date.

versions.title: Free folk: food first, and bands come in
versions.notes: Settlements now put food first: each year their head moves people onto the fields, herds and fishing boats until there is enough for everyone plus a tenth and a winter's store, and moves them back to their trades when there is plenty. This holds for every town, not just the free folk's. Hungry bands, and bands facing winter with little laid by, now head for the nearest settlement that will feed them, kin first, as long as it has food and homes to spare; most who come for the winter stay on, and the rest take to the roads again in spring. The free folk simulation is about four times faster at large scale, and the observer's speed buttons are now on every tab.

versions.title: Free folk: explorers, the land, and test sliders
versions.notes: Free folk now explore. Scouts range far and bring word of better land, bands that meet trade tales, clans share what they know, and bands move off when crowded, when fighting comes near, when they hear of much better land, or because their leader is restless. Crowded bands bud off new bands that head far away, and hunters follow the herds. They start spread over land that can actually feed them, and fight far less often, so the early slaughter and famine are gone. A new Livable map view shows the land that can feed people and where bands have been. The simulation tests now have sliders for people, world size, years, seed, violence and speed, with the presets as starting points. The free folk simulation also runs about five times faster at scale, kin no longer fight by mistake when they go by different clan names, and an emptied settlement can no longer be attacked again.

versions.title: Free folk: fixes from the first small test
versions.notes: Fixes from the first 1k simulation test. Settlements no longer get doubled names like Elmsteadstead, and bands led by someone named for a place read properly (the band of the Hollow Wood). Bands no longer fall on the settlements they founded or their kin's homes. Free folk now start spread over the better land instead of crowded onto a few regions, which ends the bloodbath and famine of the first year. The yearly count of polities now includes the free cities and leagues that break away from the realms, and the chronicle notes them rising and falling.

versions.title: Free folk part 7: the observer
versions.notes: Simulation tests can now be started whenever you like: the main menu's Simulation tests (developer key) lists the presets from content (1k, 10k and 100k free folk over 50 years), and the small test script takes -Preset. Each makes a new empty world with a dummy character at its middle and puts you in the observer's seat: you can't act in the game, only watch. The whole map is there to pan and zoom, with a button for every map view (plates, weather, anima, resonance and the rest), beside the run panel and its live charts and overviews of the free folk, the realms and the chronicle. Also fixed: the map threw errors when zoomed far out with bands on it.

versions.title: Free folk part 6: wild bands
versions.notes: Wandering bands now roam normal worlds by default. They trade with the towns they pass, and small or hungry ones settle in; hungry or wronged ones raid villages, and the realm sends patrols after them; where the law allows owning people, slavers take captives. A settlement they found inside a realm's land is the realm's. New bands come from refugees of famine and sacked towns, from peoples a realm drives out, and from tribes' kin roaming their lands. Where you meet a band you can buy food from it, recruit its hunters into your army, lead it if you have the standing, and settle it in a town of yours or beside your home. Also fixed: hungry bands never actually raided.

versions.title: Free folk part 5: watching a run
versions.notes: A simulation run screen: watch an empty world's free folk live for years, with a speed selector (steady, fast, faster, fastest), pause and step, a run panel with the year, pace and counts, six live charts (people, births and deaths, violence, wars, bands and settlements and realms, time a year), the whole world map and the major deeds as they happen. Open it from the free folk screen with Watch it run. Runs started for testing also write their yearly numbers, the chronicle, the time each system took and the graphs to files.

versions.title: Free folk part 4: conflict
versions.notes: The free folk now fight. Crowded land, old grudges, strangers of another tongue and hunger set bands and settlements against each other: skirmishes, raids for stores and captives, and rarely massacres. Every death feeds a grudge that can last years; leaders end feuds with a blood price, a marriage, a clan joined or a truce. Deep grudges between clans become wars, fought by their bands and settlements, or through the war system once both are realms; the beaten clan is conquered and joins the winner. Notable killers and famed leaders make their names. A new world setting, Their violence, from peaceful to bloody. The free folk screen shows their wars and the names to know.

versions.title: Free folk part 3: clans to realms
versions.notes: The free folk now form clans: by kinship (daughter villages, split bands), by tongue and nearness, under a strong leader, and through marriages between clans. A clan of three settlements becomes a tribe, a tribe whose seat grows into a town becomes a realm, a great leader can proclaim one sooner, and a lone town stands free. Each has a culture of its own, blended from its peoples', and its head rules it; then realms behave like any other (laws, loyalty, diplomacy, armies, wars). The free folk screen shows the clans and what they became. Also: settlements always have a head, and daughter villages a named founder.

versions.title: Free folk part 2: settling
versions.notes: Free folk now settle down. Bands discover farming and teach it to their neighbours; farming bands settle good land by water (sooner with a cautious leader or crowded land) and found real settlements that grow into hamlets and villages. In the first month or two people work into its positions: its head, offices and trades. The founders, those who made their mark and the best at each position stay known by name as its townsfolk; the rest become its people. Crowded settlements send out daughter villages, small bands of their tongue join them, and an emptied settlement is abandoned and its people roam again. The free folk screen shows their settlements. Also fixed: small settlements never grew.

versions.title: Free folk part 1: people and bands
versions.notes: A new kind of world to watch: an empty world, with no settlements, realms or threats at the start, only free folk living in roaming bands (choose World: empty in the world settings, with how many, how close and which peoples). They forage and hunt, follow game and the seasons, keep stores for winter, pair up and have children, age, and die of old age, sickness, hunger, infancy, childbirth and beasts. Bands split when too big or quarrelling and merge with their own kind. Watch them on the world map and a new free folk screen with time controls, and talk to the people of a band where you are. Normal worlds can have wandering bands too.

versions.title: Dev fix part 8: communication
versions.notes: The world has tongues: Common, one for each people, the tribes' own, old tongues and sign. Everyone speaks by their people, home and work, and talk needs a shared way: without one it's gestures, worse prices and no deep talk. Learn tongues by living among speakers, from teachers and from companions; hire interpreters (who may slant things); use the Tongues spell, scrolls or charmed items. Some people (and you, from creation or by a wound or a curse) are deaf, mute or blind, with sign, slates, ear trumpets and guides, and cures at temples, from elixirs and spells. Envoys need a shared tongue with a court. A new Language barriers world setting (off, light, full) and a tongues and senses screen. Also fixed: robbing a caravan could come away with no cargo. This is the last part of the dev fix.

versions.title: Dev fix part 7: leaders
versions.notes: You can shape your army leaders: talk with them (praise, reassure, promise, rebuke), give gifts and raises, grant titles and towns to hold, and have them mentored by you, another leader, a war school or a treatise. They grow ambitious and ask for more. The Leader drama world setting now matters more: high, they scheme for the command, feud and duel, take realms' bribes and charge for glory; low, they stay patient and steady. Realms' commanders are loyal to their ruler or not, may seize the throne or mutiny, and can be courted to come over to you or stand aside. A new leaders screen holds it all. Also fixed: some army details (leave, levies away, depots, war hosts) weren't saved.

versions.title: Dev fix part 6: sieges
versions.notes: Sieges have engines built in the camp (ladders, rams, mantlets, siege towers and trebuchets; proper ones need engineers) and plans: storm the breach, escalade, sap the walls, bombard, a night assault, or starve them out. Defenders sally and burn engines and counter-mine. A new Siege length world setting makes sieges faster or slower. Your armies can besiege towns themselves (outside a war it's a crime) and hold or sack what they take. Your own towns can lay in food, ration, repair breaches and call armies to their relief. A siege screen shows it all, with each siege's report.

versions.title: Dev fix part 5: realms at war
versions.notes: Realms make war more wisely: they strike at weak moments, seek allies first, avoid fighting on two fronts, and prepare for months with their armies gathering on the border, which everyone can see coming. In war they go for their goal and the enemy's weak points, defend their capital, seek battle when stronger and fall back when weaker, and join their armies into hosts. Peace comes when a side is spent or cuts its losses, weary allies can make a separate peace, and you can carry terms of peace between courts as an envoy for a fee from both. Realm armies are a third larger.

versions.title: Dev fix part 4: campaigning
versions.notes: Armies in the field can forage (by the land and the season), stripping the land and angering nearby towns, or eat along a supply line from your towns and from depots they leave behind; enemies can cut those lines. Winter, disease in long camps and bad weather wear armies down, and realms prefer to make war in summer. Armies can be split and merged, and bound into war hosts under a marshal that march and fight as one. New orders: escort you or your trading house's caravans, raid a settlement's land (a crime in peacetime), and retreat to your nearest town.

versions.title: Dev fix part 3: raising and keeping armies
versions.notes: Soldiers need real gear: spears, shields, mail, bows and horses come from your stores or the town's market (realms buy theirs too), and without it levies come poorly armed until re-armed. Gear wears out in battle and in the field. Armies drill in towns (rest, drill or hard drill), faster with a drillmaster and training grounds, a new town building and home room. Levies cost their towns: fields go short at sowing and harvest, long absences sour the mood, and the fallen are mourned. Levies can go home on leave and be called back, or be rotated for fresh ones. New goods: spears, mail, bows and shields.

versions.title: Dev fix part 2: battles
versions.notes: Battles have plans (hold the line, all-out attack, feigned retreat, turning the flanks, ambush), each with its strengths, the ground it needs and the plans it counters; commanders choose by their nature and good tacticians read the enemy's. Armies form lines: a centre, two flanks, a reserve and a rear, by unit kind, by the plan, or as you place each unit, and an open flank gets turned. A battle of your army where you are opens the battle screen: watch it phase by phase or decide between phases (commit the reserve, rally, charge now, change the plan, retreat in order). You can lead an army yourself and fight in its line with your companions. Better generals matter more, at dusk the side in better heart holds the field, and every report can be replayed.

versions.title: Dev fix part 1: army settings, pay and morale
versions.notes: Four new world settings under War, each in five steps and changeable in play: army cost, war frequency, war scale and leader drama. Army morale now swings with victories and defeats, pay, food, rest, the march, the weather, the commander and spoils, each reason shown on the army screen and editable in content. Low morale brings deserters, armies that refuse their orders, and mutiny; unpaid, hungry soldiers may loot your own towns. Armies can be paid in full, half in spoils, or in plunder, and mercenaries can sign on for a cut of the spoils.

versions.title: M19 part 9: the last of M19's systems
versions.notes: The ninth and last part of M19's systems is in this build.

versions.title: M19 part 8: summons with a self
versions.notes: Your elemental and familiars become beings of their own: each gains a name, a nature and an opinion of you, remembers what you did together, and grows stronger with fights and time (new moves at higher levels). Your elemental stays the same being in every element. Talk with them, thank them, reshape them, bind a soul from your gems into one (it takes on who that soul was), send them on errands (scouting, gathering, listening), to live at your home, or with your army. How many you can hold grows with your evocation; they draw on your mana's recovery, and a being that comes to resent you slips its bond. Slain, they reform weaker for a while, remembering.

versions.title: M19 part 7: servitude
versions.notes: Ownership and servitude go deeper. The people you own have fear and loyalty as well as obedience: fear makes them comply but eats loyalty; the loyal never run and may refuse freedom. Train them, put them to work in your trading house or hire them out to the mines, take them along (the frightened may run in a lost fight). Runaways leave a trail you can hunt; unhappy households may rise up; liberators come where it is forbidden; the owned save towards buying their freedom, and the freed remember how they were treated. Black markets sell people where it isn't legal; slavers can be hired, and they hunt the roads; your armies' victories bring captives; trade in people is taxed. Rulers can decree the law on owning people. A new dark setting (off by default) lets you break the people you own, and lets slavers take you captive.

versions.title: M19 part 6
versions.notes: The sixth part of M19's systems is in this build. Bound spirits can also live on resonance-rich reagents when crystal runs out.

versions.title: M19 part 5: lineage
versions.notes: Families: married couples have children, who grow up in about three months of play. Choose how each is raised (letters, arms, a trade, magic, faith), foster them away, and spend time with them: grown, they become people of the world, fond of you and at your side, or estranged rivals. They marry (or you arrange a match into a noble house) and have children of their own. Your house gains renown; name your heir. You age too, and in old age your years run out: you go on as your heir, who inherits what you had. A new start, Married with an heir; and priests may give a foundling a home with you. The party screen has a Family view.

versions.title: M19 part 4
versions.notes: The fourth part of M19's systems is in this build. People you haven't met for a while now keep what has happened between you.

versions.title: M19 part 3: relationships
versions.notes: Relationships: everyone you know has affection and commitment towards you, and what you are to each other follows from them (friend, sweetheart, partner, betrothed, spouse, or rival). Spend time together, pay compliments, give gifts they like and go out together; high charisma helps a great deal. Ask them to be with you, propose, and hold the wedding in a town, where each realm's law says how many spouses you may have and whether a marriage can end. People expect to be the only one, or not, by their nature: those who do grow jealous of your others, unless you talk them round. Your companions and household form friendships, romances and grudges of their own, and party morale follows. Matters of the heart are in conversation; the party screen has a Relationships view.

versions.title: M19 part 2
versions.notes: The second part of M19's systems is in this build.

versions.title: M19 part 1
versions.notes: The first part of M19's systems is in this build. Fixed: your mod list (which mods are on and their order) now applies from the moment the game starts, not only after you change it.

versions.title: M19 groundwork 5: the travelling herd
versions.notes: Your livestock can travel with you as a herd: how many you can drive grows with husbandry, and the herd slows you a little. It grazes where there is grass, else eats its feed from your packs, and gives its milk, eggs and wool into them. Watch it: beasts stray on the road (search for them), one may be taken at camp unless you sit up with them, and left alone they drift away, unless a town's herder minds them for a fee. Pen them at home and take them out again; buy into the herd and sell from it at markets. The Herder start now begins with two goats. The trades' numbers are now set in the game's content files.

versions.title: M19 groundwork 4: versions to install
versions.notes: The version list now offers the newest version, the last version of each phase, and a few selected ones to install (for now the last of M15, M16, M17 and M18). Versions you already have installed stay in the list and can be switched to and away from as before. If some game content fails to load, a notice says so (try turning mods off).

versions.title: M19 groundwork 3: trades and Presence
versions.notes: Presence, a new fighting school of charisma: rebukes, taunts, stares and commands wear down a foe's resolve until they give up the fight, and a rally lifts your whole side. Two trades join the schools: Performer (play any inn for coin and goodwill, hear the room's talk, and talk your way to better prices at every counter; a lute helps) and Husbandry (your animals give more, eat less, forage, breed in their pens, and cost less to buy). With extended creation, Starting trades lets you begin as a performer, a herder or a cradle keeper.

versions.title: M19 groundwork 2: resonance cradles
versions.notes: Pulse gems grow in resonance cradles: crystal bowls that hum with your resonance while you carry them. The gem trader sells them, or make one at a gem bench from four veyrite shards and an ingot. Set a seed crystal in one from your inventory and it grows through the usual stages; each cradle holds one gem, and gem tending lets you tend more. Gem halls let you tend a seed for them with your own cradle, for a fee.

versions.title: M19 groundwork 1: content loading
versions.notes: Groundwork for M19: how the game's content is organised and loaded. The siren of the fracture zones now sings a lulling song that drags at you, and the About screen has credits.

versions.title: M18 part 5: the mod format
versions.notes: Mods get a proper home. Each mod can carry a manifest (name, version, author, what it needs and what it loads after), and the new Mods screen in the main menu lists them in load order with their status and any errors: turn them on or off and move them up or down, and the content reloads at once. Mods can patch the game instead of copying whole entries (set a field, add to or remove from a list, delete an entry), bring icons and text tables, and saves remember which mods they were made with, warning you before loading with different ones. Two sample mods come next to the game, off until you turn them on: The Wandering Tinker and The Tinker's Road, which needs it. M18 is complete.

versions.title: M18 part 4: discovery and investigation
versions.notes: Mysteries to solve: ask people what they know (freely if they trust you, or pay, persuade or lean on them), search where it happened, and name the culprit by your own judgement; name the wrong one and the innocent pays. Cases come from real misdeeds townsfolk actually committed, from thefts among the needs, and from an authored case at Greyfall, the alchemist's missing ledger. What becomes of the guilty is yours to decide: the watch, a bribe, a hold over them, mercy, or exile. Quests also find you: rumours at the inn, a letter in a dungeon hoard, bones in a ruin, a soul's unfinished business; and they lead on to others. Outcomes now decide people's fates, a town's mood and a court's favour.

versions.title: M18 part 3: quests from the living world
versions.notes: Every settlement now has a few needs of its own, worked out only when someone asks (so huge worlds stay fast): a dungeon troubling the town, a beast near it, someone gone missing toward a ruin, goods it lacks, a debt called in, a quarrel between neighbours to settle. People who think well of you ask for help when you talk to them, others tell you of a neighbour's trouble (a lead in the journal), and the notice board lists what is posted. Adventuring parties race you for some of them: if they finish first, the work is theirs, and whoever you let down remembers.

versions.title: M18 part 2: authored quest lines
versions.notes: Quest lines written as scenes: roles found from anchors, people and each other (the ruin nearest the waystation, the innkeeper, the guard), scenes that play when you reach a quest's place, several ways through (alternative objectives, skill checks in scenes, endings by the way taken), and moral choices that are remembered by the people involved, spread as word, read by later quests and felt by realms. Rewards can now be land, a title, a knighthood, a follower or a home. The first line: The Lantern's lost wagons, offered at the Lantern Inn of Greyfall Waystation.

versions.title: M18 part 1: quests and the journal
versions.notes: Quests arrive: written as data with roles filled from the world, stages, objectives (go, talk, bring, slay, clear, defend, learn, find, follow, or any condition), branches, deadlines, rewards, and failures that can sometimes be put right. The journal (J) gathers your quests and every task you hold: guild contracts, mercenary jobs, court tasks, your company's contract, errands, rulers' calls, bounties, commissions and supply contracts. Filter and sort them, read each one's next step, time left, reward and notes, track one (its next step in the side panel, its place marked on the maps), and look back on your history. A sample quest: console `quest`.

versions.title: M17 part 8b: spies
versions.notes: Work in the shadows of other realms: spy out what a realm hides (its treasury, armies, wavering lords and plots), bribe, flatter or blackmail its lords against their ruler, forge insults, fan grudges or sabotage treaties at its court (or calm it towards peace), burn stores, poison wells, open a besieged town's gates, and murder a lord or the ruler. Every covert act risks being caught, against your stealth and disguise and the realm's spymaster: a bounty, your name, and the realm you speak for blamed, a cause for war. Realms' own spies work against their rivals; ruling, you judge the ones caught in your realm (hang, release or turn them). M17 is complete.

versions.title: M17 part 8a: envoys
versions.notes: Speak for the realm you serve or rule at other courts: negotiate treaties for it (your charisma and your name add to their regard), broker treaties or a peace between two others for a fee from each, carry word between courts (messages, gifts that warm, ultimatums that chill; gifts can be robbed on the road), and speak against a court's neighbours. Serving, ask your court for an embassy or word to carry. Words between courts fade month by month, and realms send envoys of their own.

versions.title: M17 part 7b: statecraft and projects
versions.notes: Rule your realm's dealings: treaties others offer come to your court, you propose and break treaties, declare wars for a goal, demand terms or offer peace, and set your armies' doctrine. And projects steer how realms grow: rulers call on the common people (bring goods to the seat, slay a threat, clear a dungeon), on settlement owners (build what a town lacks, more hands in a trade, more output, the most of a trade, a rising ended) or on polities (a treaty), paying from the treasury per unit or as a prize. Answer other realms' calls yourself, or post your own when you rule.

versions.title: M17 part 7a: ruling a realm
versions.notes: Rule a realm now. Seize the throne where you hold land (a coup if you are strong enough, a rebellion if not), break away with the settlements you head, found a realm of your own, or be elected, acclaimed or named heir where you serve. As ruler, what would happen of itself comes to your court: your chancellor's decrees, lords asking for land, feuds, plots uncovered; decide, or let your officers settle them. Issue decrees, reward and strip lords, fill offices, draw on the treasury. You can lose it as any ruler does: a coup, a rising, an election, conquest. Your diplomacy, wars and projects come next.

versions.title: M17 part 6b: soldiering
versions.notes: Enlist in a realm's army when you stand beside it: you march with it wherever it goes, fight in its battles (and are sometimes hurt), draw its pay, and rise from soldier to sergeant to officer. Leave with an honourable discharge while it rests, or desert and be hunted. With an army of your own, realms at war near you offer to hire your company for months at a time: take the contract, answer their call, and draw their pay until the term or the war is done.

versions.title: M17 part 6a: serving a ruler
versions.notes: Serve a ruler now. Your renown with a realm grows with what its people know of you, threats you slay in its land and tasks you do for it. Swear fealty at its seat, or be invited for your deeds to a position that fits you: its service, command, or an office at court. In its service your favour rises and falls with what you do: answer its calls to war by lending your army to its host, take tasks from court (lift a siege, slay a threat, clear a dungeon), show yourself at court. Rewards: pay and purses, a knighthood, land of your own (you become its lord), offices, pardons. Fall too low and you are dismissed. Enlisting as a soldier and mercenary contracts come next.

versions.title: M17 part 5: sieges
versions.notes: Walled settlements are besieged now. The besiegers cut them off: their stores run down day by day, siege works and engines breach the walls, sickness thins both sides, the defenders sally. When the walls are breached, a gate is opened, or the town starves and surrenders, it falls, and its conqueror's commander decides: hold it, free its people if they are kin, or sack it (plunder, people killed and fled, buildings burned, a hatred that lasts years). Caught inside, you can't walk out: slip through the lines by night, man the walls, or open a gate for the besiegers for a reward. Food grows dear while it lasts.

versions.title: M17 part 4: war
versions.notes: Realms go to war now. A realm that regards a neighbour badly enough, and is strong enough with its allies, declares war for land it claims, to bring the other to heel, for revenge, or to swallow it whole (a war without a cause costs honour and its lords' loyalty). Allies join or refuse at a price. Realm armies storm settlements (one battle against the walls for now; sieges come next), take their own back and meet enemy armies in the field. Battles and settlements taken build a war score, losses and months weariness, and peace comes on terms that follow: land ceded, vassalage, reparations, or a realm swallowed. See each realm's wars on the realm screen.

versions.title: M17 part 3: diplomacy
versions.notes: Realms regard their neighbours now, for reasons you can read: shared borders, land taken and kin held down, old grudges and broken treaties, how each treats the other's peoples, alike or opposed governments, embargoes, ambitious rulers, good faith. Their stances follow. Neighbours make trade pacts (half the tariffs), non-aggression pacts, defensive and full alliances, royal marriages, vassalage and tribute, and break them when regard sours, at a cost to their honour.
