Each realm's claims on another are the causes for the wars to come. See it under Relations on the realm screen.

versions.title: M17 part 2: realm armies
versions.notes: Realms field armies of their own now. Each ruler chooses a doctrine: a standing army paid from the treasury, levies raised when needed, or a mix. When a threat comes near, a rising grows or a lord rebels, the realm sends its standing army or musters one: its lords answer the call by their loyalty (or refuse), conscripts come by its conscription law, mercenaries if it is rich. Rebel lords are met in the field and crushed, or break away if they hold out. Idle standing armies guard the borders. See them on the realm screen and the map.

versions.title: M17 part 1: lords and holdings
versions.notes: Realms are held by lords now: dukes, counts and barons in a monarchy, governors under a dictator, great houses in an oligarchy, elected magistrates in a republic, prelates in a theocracy, clan chiefs and village councils. Each settlement outside the ruler's own is a lord's, nested under greater lords. Lords keep a share of their taxes, their loyalty sways the ruler's decrees and their towns, and they seek to rise, feud with rivals, plot for the throne (seizing it or breaking away), and build wealth and retinues. Head a lord's seat and its rents are yours. See it on the realm screen.

versions.title: M16 part 6: leaders as people
versions.notes: Your commanders are people now. Their loyalty to your command and their friendship with you feed each other: friends start loyal and forgive more, but a long bad command wears the friendship down. Victories, losses, pay, hunger, captives left unransomed, rivals and being passed over move their loyalty, each by their nature. The discontented grumble, ask for another post, resign, and rarely do worse: desert with followers, go rogue as a warlord, sell your plans, or take the whole army. Leaders grow with battles, earn renown and names like Dragonbane or the Unbroken, and rivals in one command work against each other. M16 is complete.

versions.title: M16 part 5: battles
versions.notes: Your armies now fight real battles: scouting decides who strikes first, then volleys, a charge and rounds of melee, with counters, morale, the ground and the weather all counting. Each foe is a host of its kind (brigands, rebels, warbands, great beasts, dragons, the restless dead, dungeon hosts). The wounded recover, survivors grow seasoned, and a beaten army may lose its leaders to captivity until you ransom them. Bandits ambush armies in the field, and you can send an army to put down a rising in a town you head. Every battle is kept as a report you can read phase by phase.

versions.title: M16 part 4: armies on the map
versions.notes: Send your armies out: march to a settlement, garrison or patrol around one (the land nearby grows safer), defend a town against threats that come near, hunt a threat the guild knows of, or clear a dungeon. They march day by day, shown on the world map, eat the rations they carry in the field and buy more in towns, go hungry when they run out, and fight what they were sent against (a single exchange for now; full battles come next). Each army keeps a log.

versions.title: M16 part 3: advisors and specialists
versions.notes: Attach advisors to your leaders (a strategist, a quartermaster who lets them hold more soldiers, a spymaster, an orator who keeps morale up, a war mage) and specialists who strengthen unit types (cavalry master, master archer, battle magister, golem warden, necromancer, chief surgeon, siege engineer). Their own skill decides how much they help; each leader has slots by rank and leadership.

versions.title: M16 part 2: leaders and capacity
versions.notes: You never command: appoint a commander and sub-commanders for each army from your companions, your household, the notables of settlements you head, and captains for hire in towns and cities. New skills tactics and logistics. Each leader commands so many soldiers; armies grow from warband to army to grand army and need sub-commanders as they do; past capacity an army fights weaker, frays and wastes.

versions.title: M16 part 1: troops and the roster
versions.notes: Raise your own armies: unit types from militia to heavy cavalry, battle mages and field surgeons, with peoples' variants (dwarf shield walls, elf longbows, centaur riders and lancers…). Levy soldiers in settlements you head (they leave its people and go home when dismissed) and hire mercenary companies in towns and cities; pay and rations every month, or morale falls and soldiers leave. Leaders, orders, marching and battles come in the next parts. Saves are version 50.

versions.title: M15 part 19b: your part at the halls
versions.notes: Work a week at a town's incubation halls as an attuner, harvester or refiner, paid by your gem skills; host for a hall (its attuners set a seed in you and pay a fee; the gem is yours); sell pulse gems at markets by grade; pay for a town's hall and own it, with a monthly share of its gems (none where the realm runs its halls). This completes M15. Saves are version 49.

versions.title: M15 part 19a: incubation halls
versions.notes: Towns raise incubation halls where their realm's pulse gem policy allows, with nurseries, ley chambers and wings. Their hosts grow cultivated gems by grade (lesser, common, greater, grand) into the markets, cheaper where halls stand; bought, a gem carries its town's peoples' imprint. Realms decree the policy: prohibited, regulated, a free market, state halls or coerced.

versions.title: M15 part 18b: movers and movements
versions.notes: Where a realm's towns seethe, a people is held down or far towns chafe, a mover rises: a notable who leads a revolt, a rising or a secession. Their movement gathers the angriest towns; its rulers crack down, give ground or spread propaganda; it wins (a new government with its leader as ruler, a people freed, a free city), fails (its leader gone for good) or stalls into a breakaway. Raise one yourself, support it, join it, take its lead or inform on it. Saves are version 48.

versions.title: M15 part 18a: unrest, removal and elections
versions.notes: Each of a town's peoples and classes has its own discontent (hunger, taxes and the levy, decrees, how their people are treated, their head's standing), rising through grumbling and petitions to protests and riots that burn its fund and its loyalty. A town that calls for its head long enough has them removed by its realm's law (its council, the lord above, its people), and its notables stand for the seat by standing and endorsements. Stir a town up, join or break its protests, stand for an open seat and win endorsements. Saves are version 47.

versions.title: M15 part 17c: your say
versions.notes: Petition a realm's ruler at its seat for any decree it could issue (a gift by its rank; your standing, charisma and an office in the realm make it likelier). Set your own steading's rules (dues, a curfew, market rules), or propose them where you hold an office. Lobby a realm through your guild for its charter, lower tariffs or an end to an embargo. Saves are version 46.

versions.title: M15 part 17b: laws that bite you
versions.notes: Crimes the watch learns of are fined (paid at any town of the realm); unpaid fines and grave crimes make you wanted: guards stop you at its gates (pay, the cells, fight or run) and bounty hunters find you on its roads. Realms tax your market sales; your home's realm may call you to its levy (serve or pay); schools of magic under licence need one bought there, and banned ones are crimes. The settlement screen shows the law there. Saves are version 45.

versions.title: M15 part 17a: decrees and policies
versions.notes: Realms set their taxes, conscription and tariffs, license or ban each school of magic, and embargo hostile neighbours, by decrees their rulers issue as their government, treasury, magic and unrest allow. Taxes fill a realm's treasury out of its towns' takings and cost it mood and loyalty; the levy feeds its garrisons; tariffs and embargoes steer its merchants; decrees stir unrest that fades. The Realms screen shows each realm's laws and policies. Saves are version 44.

versions.title: M15 part 16b: offices of your own
versions.notes: Seek a town's office (steward, captain of the watch, priest, magister) where you stand well and your people are citizens, with a gift to its head: your attributes are your skill, you choose its focus and draw its pay, and bad years or months away lose it. Head your own steading: appoint its officers from candidates, choose what it builds next, draw on its fund. Once a year, an audience with a town's head: advise them on its weakest stat, or petition for a building. Saves are version 43.

versions.title: M15 part 16a: governance
versions.notes: Every settlement has a head by its tier and government (a village elder, a reeve or mayor, a governor or lord mayor, a chief, a commander; a realm's seat is its ruler's), and towns and cities have a steward, a captain of the watch, a priest and a magister, held by its people. Their skill shapes how the town fares: food, housing, prosperity, mood, order, safety and magic, shown on the settlement screen. Prosperity fills the building fund, a good steward builds for less, a priest lifts the mood, low order brings unrest and cutpurses, and the watch makes the roads near town safer.

versions.title: M15 part 15c: outposts, forts and castles
versions.notes: Realms near you raise outposts on roads at their borders (passes best), named for the nearest town. Their garrisons grow with their realm and more with hostile neighbours, and with the buildings they need an outpost becomes a fort and a fort a castle. Their realm feeds them and pays for their building, and their patrols make the roads around them safer. Each has its own map and a garrison scene.

versions.title: M15 part 15b: buildings on the town map
versions.notes: Settlement maps have lots by district where their buildings stand (inn and market doors, the smithy, a temple, a granary, a watchtower) and empty lots to build on; what a town builds or you pay for appears on its map. Steadings, hamlets and cities have maps of their own, and a settlement that changes tier takes its new tier's map.

versions.title: M15 part 15a: settlement growth and tiers
versions.notes: Settlements grow and dwindle between tiers (steading, hamlet, village, town, city), with buildings by district: homes cap growth, granaries soften famine, services and defence. They build from their takings and lose buildings in hard years. Pay for a building anywhere you are; bring settlers to farm the land by your home.

versions.title: M15 part 14: the magic economy
versions.notes: Realm laws on four magical practices (warded fields, transmutation, golem labour, weather-working), from each culture and changed by rulers' decrees. They feed on Pulse crystals, reagents and essences (mana carries them a little way), make magic towns' markets follow their magic more than their stores, and you can serve a town's practice for pay. A Magic map view.

versions.title: M15 part 13b: prototyping
versions.notes: Design new goods from parts (usefulness, novelty, quality, cost), make prototypes and show them: word of mouth spreads town to town. Sell a design, or win a charter from your guild or a realm so workshops make it and pay you royalties; unprotected designs get copied.

versions.title: M15 part 13a: your trade
versions.notes: Haul goods yourself in carts and wagons (cargo by weight, a slower pace, teams to feed, bandits). Found a trading house and send its caravans out as merchants, with monthly accounts. Commissions from people, supply contracts from towns (your house can fulfil them), and smuggling past realm patrols.

versions.title: M15 part 12, intrigue reworked
versions.notes: Gossip reworked for speed: who saw a deed keeps it as a secret (whether and when they talk is settled when they learn it), and common knowledge follows rumour curves worked out when asked instead of a daily simulation, about 50 times faster. Old deeds nobody holds are forgotten. Merchant caravans no longer slow down big worlds.

versions.title: M15 part 12: merchant guilds
versions.notes: Merchant guilds founded in cities, with halls in the towns around them. Members share price news, ride in convoys, keep guild prices and win charters from rulers; rival guilds feud over routes. Join one at its hall, take its contracts, rise from apprentice to elder and vote on its feuds; cross one and its halls shut you out.

versions.title: M15 part 11: merchant caravans
versions.notes: Merchants travel the road near you as caravans with their real cargo and guards. Roads cost danger, guards and losses; borders take tariffs; a realm's roads take tolls (from you too); ports' merchants sail between ports. Trade with a caravan, guard it to market for pay, or rob it.

versions.title: M15 part 10: merchants
versions.notes: Merchants run between markets, carrying what is plentiful at one end and dear at the other: imports and exports move prices and feed the hungry. Their businesses grow or fail year by year. Talk to merchants about their trade and sell them news of markets; a Trade map view.

versions.title: M15 part 9: markets and prices
versions.notes: Every settlement is a market: prices follow its stores and needs, your trading moves them; market stalls, smiths and inns draw on it; trends, the markets you know and a Prices map view. Masterpieces sell at city auction halls and to collectors; makers in the world grow famous, and so do you.

versions.title: M15 part 8: consumption and demand
versions.notes: Settlements' people by class need food, clothing, fuel, salt, drink and more, by their peoples' diets; hunger drives people away, famine kills, want lowers loyalty to the realm, plenty lets a town grow. A Prosperity map view, how a settlement fares in its economy screen and scenes, news of famines and booms.

versions.title: M15 part 7: production
versions.notes: Every settlement works its land with trades that follow it (farmers, herders, fishers, foresters, miners, millers, weavers...), feeds itself first and makes what its land does best; harvests at summer's end; a settlement economy screen, a Production map view, harvest time in villages, mines working for their towns.

versions.title: M15 part 6: goods and masterpieces
versions.notes: 1,008 trade goods (crops, animals, land, made, magical), each tied to its items and to where it comes from; a Goods view on the world map and a goods codex; 248 new crafts with a craft row in towns; masterpieces: one-of-a-kind named pieces whose worth moves with their history.

versions.title: M15 part 5c: choosing where to begin, ruling families
versions.notes: When the world is made, pick where to begin on its map (crosshairs on every place your origin can start). The noble origins become ruling families: choose the kind of polity your family rules in; your house fits it, and the realm takes that government and your kind as citizens.

versions.title: M15 part 5b: endless worlds, origin starts
versions.notes: Unlimited worlds go on in every direction without seams, made as you travel, beginning at the nearest land with room to live; climate bands repeat every 2,560 km. Each origin begins at its own place: a town, a farming village, a fringe village, a city, a noble's own manor.

versions.title: M15 part 5a: loading in layers, huge and vast worlds
versions.notes: Huge (512) and vast (1024) worlds, sketched whole and drawn near you; a loading screen showing each layer being made; worlds up to large unchanged.

versions.title: M15 part 4: realms and settlements from the land
versions.notes: Settlements where the land feeds them; realms, free cities and tribes with governments, stances towards every people and a history; borders that move.

versions.title: M15 part 3: geology and soil
versions.notes: Bedrock from the plates, soils, timber, mineral deposits, mines and quarries; prospecting, working the land, smelting and alloying.

versions.title: M15 part 2: climate and water
versions.notes: Climate by latitude, height and sea; wind belts, rain shadows, monsoons; rivers to great rivers; biomes from climate; snow, frozen rivers and exposure.

versions.title: M15 part 1: plates, resonance and anima
versions.notes: Worlds from tectonic plates: ranges, passes, volcanoes, rifts, inland seas; the resonance and anima maps; bigger worlds.

versions.title: M14: overworld and parties
versions.notes: Your party (roles, morale, mounts, food, camping), and groups on the road: caravans, pilgrims, patrols, bandits and warbands.

versions.title: M13: souls, anima gems and constructs
versions.notes: Soul harvesting and anima gems, constructs and their parts, souled constructs, beings of pure soul, speaking with the dead.

versions.title: M12: home and household
versions.notes: Claim and build a home, a household with jobs and rules, and owned people and entities (content setting).

versions.title: M11.5: knowledge, secrets and intrigue
versions.notes: Deeds and witnesses, gossip that travels, rumours, informants, blackmail and silencing.

versions.title: M11: dungeons, guilds and the Dungeon Master
versions.notes: Dungeons that grow, threats, the Adventurers' and Mercenaries' Guilds, NPC parties, and the Dungeon Master school.

versions.title: M10: personal combat
versions.notes: Turn-based combat with action points, telegraphed intents, conditions, summons and believable loot.

versions.title: M9: simulation at scale
versions.notes: The people of the world: schedules, needs, detail tiers; opinions, companions and conversation.

versions.title: M8: the world
versions.notes: A generated overworld with anchors, tile-map locations, travel, weather, danger and encounters.

versions.title: M7: resonance and pulse gems
versions.notes: Pulse gems: natural gems, incubation in a host, charging, refining, gems as spell fuel.

versions.title: M6.5: character creation, extended
versions.notes: Content and game settings, schools and spell trees, and the six pages of character creation.

versions.title: M6: body, magic and resonance
versions.notes: Bodies and transformation; spells, schools, potions, enchanting and tattoos.

versions.title: M5: gathering and crafting
versions.notes: Gathering nodes, tools, refining chains, recipes, quality and workstations.

versions.title: M4: items and equipment
versions.notes: Inventory, layered equipment, materials and shops.

versions.title: M3: time, effects and saves
versions.notes: The calendar and clock, status effects, regeneration, saving and loading.

versions.title: M2: characters
versions.notes: Characters, attributes, the character sheet and creation.

versions.title: M1: text and scenes
versions.notes: Scenes, choices, hotkeys and templated text.

versions.title: M0: skeleton
versions.notes: The first build: content loading, hot reload and the debug console.
